claims.text: A hybrid machine-learned interatomic potential with selective ab initio corrections can accurately capture solid and liquid free energies near fusion.
The proposed method can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The ML potential will be trained using sparse ab initio data.
Interleaving ML simulations with on-the-fly ab initio corrections will keep the relevant entropy and coupling contributions accurate.
The method will first be tested on elemental and binary systems near their melting points and then extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
ML potentials have shown promising transferability in prior elemental or binary studies.
Traditional free-energy methods slow down for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The ML potential mediates the method by reproducing the atomic interaction landscape.
Active learning guarantees that configurations critical to phase transitions are corrected by targeted ab initio calculations.
Reducing the number of ab initio calculations through an adaptive ML potential will enable rapid prediction of solid–liquid free-energy differences.
Active learning will dynamically correct deviations caused by anomalous electron–vibration coupling or anharmonic effects.
The method will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD.
Predicted phase free energies and derived observables will agree with ab initio and TOR-TILD benchmarks within ±5%.
Full AIMD and TOR-TILD free-energy calculations are computationally intensive, particularly for multicomponent systems.
The expected validity domain includes benchmarked elemental and binary systems and modestly complex multicomponent alloys near melting.
Extreme compositional complexity or temperatures far from melting may require revalidation and recalibration of the ML potential.
